content: Erythromycin is an antibiotic used to treat a wide range of bacterial infections. It may also be prescribed to prevent certain bacterial infections. This medication belongs to the macrolide class of antibiotics and is effective only against bacterial infections; it does not work for viral infections such as the common cold or flu. To use erythromycin, take it by mouth as directed by your doctor, usually before a meal. It is best absorbed on an empty stomach. Do not crush the medication, as it has a bitter taste; swallow it whole. The dosage and duration of treatment depend on your medical condition and response to therapy. For optimal results, take this antibiotic at evenly spaced intervals. If you are using it to treat an infection, continue taking it for the full prescribed duration, even if symptoms improve after a few days. Stopping the medication too early may allow the infection to return. If you are taking it to prevent an infection, follow your doctor’s instructions precisely. Common side effects of erythromycin include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach pain or cramping, and loss of appetite. Taking the medication with food may help reduce these symptoms. Remember that this medication has been prescribed because your doctor has determined that the benefits outweigh the risks of side effects. Rarely, erythromycin may cause a severe intestinal condition due to a bacteria called Clostridium difficile (C. difficile). This condition can occur during treatment or weeks to months after treatment has stopped. Prolonged or repeated use of this medication may lead to oral thrush or a new yeast infection. Serious allergic reactions to erythromycin are rare but possible. Erythromycin may cause a condition that affects the heart rhythm, known as QT prolongation. This risk is higher if you have certain medical conditions or are taking other medications that can cause QT prolongation. Low levels of potassium or magnesium in the blood can also increase this risk, especially if you are using diuretics (water pills) or experiencing severe sweating, diarrhea, or vomiting. Additionally, erythromycin may interfere with the effectiveness of live bacterial vaccines, such as the typhoid vaccine. Some erythromycin products may contain sodium, and the medication can pass into breast milk. Drug interactions can alter how erythromycin or other medications work, potentially increasing the risk of serious side effects. Keep a list of all the products you use, including prescription and non-prescription drugs and herbal supplements, and share it with your doctor and pharmacist. Other medications may affect the removal of erythromycin from your body, impacting its effectiveness. Similarly, erythromycin can slow the removal of other drugs from your body, affecting how they work. This medication may also interfere with certain laboratory tests, such as urine tests, potentially causing false results. If someone overdoses on erythromycin and experiences severe symptoms such as passing out or difficulty breathing, call emergency services (911) immediately. Otherwise, contact a poison control center right away. In the U.S., you can call 1-800-222-1222. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is near the time of your next dose, skip the missed dose and resume your regular dosing schedule. Do not double the dose to catch up. Store erythromycin at room temperature, away from light and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Do not flush medications down the toilet or pour them into a drain unless instructed to do so. Properly discard this product when it is expired or no longer needed. This information is a summary and does not include all possible details about erythromycin. It does not guarantee that the medication is safe, effective, or appropriate for you. Always consult your healthcare professional for complete information about this product and your specific health needs.
